docs.title: 🎯 Objectives & Scope
docs.text:
Approximate computing trades strict arithmetic accuracy for significant reductions in power consumption, silicon area, and critical path delay in error-resilient applications such as: - Deep Learning / Neural Network Accelerators (Conv2D, GEMM, Transformer attention) - Computer Vision & Image Processing (Filtering, Edge detection, JPEG/HEVC compression) - Signal Processing & Wireless Communications (FFT, FIR, CORDIC coordinate rotations)

This portal synthesizes knowledge extracted from 582+ peer-reviewed papers, 585+ reproducible baseline work packages, and standardized multi-PDK synthesis results.

docs.title: Glossary of Inexact & Approximate Computing
docs.text: This glossary provides concise, plain-English definitions and mathematical context for terms frequently used across approximate hardware design.

docs.title: Accuracy-Configurable / Dual-Mode
docs.text: An arithmetic unit that can switch at runtime between exact computation mode and one or more approximate modes to dynamically adapt to varying battery, thermal, or QoS constraints.

docs.title: Carry-Disregard / Broken-Array
docs.text: A multiplier optimization technique where carry propagation is cut or disregarded in the least significant bit (LSB) columns of the partial product reduction tree, eliminating long carry-chains at the cost of bounded LSB error.

docs.title: Compressor (Approximate 4:2 / 5:2)
docs.text: A multi-input adder cell used in Wallace/Dadda trees that condenses \(N\) partial product bits into sum and carry outputs with simplified Boolean logic that introduces rare, low-magnitude truth-table deviations.

docs.title: DRUM (Dynamic Range Unbiased Multiplier)
docs.text: A leading-one detector (LOD) based multiplier that dynamically selects a \(k\)-bit window of the most significant active bits of operands, truncating lower bits while applying unbiased rounding compensation.

docs.title: EDP (Energy-Delay Product)
docs.text: A primary hardware figure-of-merit defined as \(\text{EDP} = \text{Energy} \times \text{Delay} = \text{Power} \times \text{Delay}^2\).

docs.title: ER (Error Rate)
docs.text: The fraction of all input combinations for which the approximate circuit output differs from the exact mathematical result: $\(\text{ER} = \frac{1}{|S|} \sum_{x \in S} \mathbb{I}(Y_{approx}(x) \neq Y_{exact}(x))\)$

docs.title: Lower-Part Constant (LPC)
docs.text: An approximation scheme in adders or multipliers where the \(k\) least significant bits of the result are fixed to a constant (often \(2^{k-1}\)) or trivial bitwise OR, reducing area to zero in the lower slice.

docs.title: MED (Mean Error Distance)
docs.text: The average absolute arithmetic error over the input evaluation domain \(S\): $\(\text{MED} = \frac{1}{|S|} \sum_{x \in S} |Y_{approx}(x) - Y_{exact}(x)|\)$

docs.title: MRED (Mean Relative Error Distance)
docs.text: The average relative error across non-zero exact outputs, crucial for signal processing where relative precision matters more than absolute magnitude: $\(\text{MRED} = \frac{1}{|S \setminus \{x: Y_{exact}=0\}|} \sum \frac{|Y_{approx}(x) - Y_{exact}(x)|}{|Y_{exact}(x)|}\)$

docs.title: NMED (Normalized Mean Error Distance)
docs.text: \(\text{MED}\) normalized by the maximum possible output \(D_{max}\) of the exact circuit: $\(\text{NMED} = \frac{\text{MED}}{D_{max}}\)$

docs.title: RoBA (Rounding-Based Approximate Multiplier)
docs.text: An algorithm that rounds operands to their nearest powers of two (\(A \approx 2^{k_1}, B \approx 2^{k_2}\)), performing multiplication via barrel shifters and basic subtraction rather than full multiplier trees.

docs.title: WCE (Worst-Case Error)
docs.text: The maximum absolute error magnitude that the approximate circuit can produce across the entire input space: $\(\text{WCE} = \max_{x \in S} |Y_{approx}(x) - Y_{exact}(x)|\)$

docs.title: 3. Design Selection Heuristic
docs.text:
1. For High-Fidelity Signal & Image Processing (\(PSNR > 35\text{ dB}\)):
  2. Choose Approximate 4:2 Compressors or TOSAM with small truncation.
  3. For Edge DNN Inference (Quantized INT8 / MobileNet):
  4. Choose DRUM-5/6 or Logarithmic multipliers (retains \(>98\%\) top-1 accuracy).
  5. For Extreme Energy-Constrained IoT / Bio-Sensors:
  6. Choose RoBA or Broken-Array Multipliers (BAM) for \(>70\%\) energy savings.

docs.title: Why Artificial Intelligence Loves Inexact Math
docs.text:
Large AI models—from ChatGPT to self-driving vision systems (YOLO, ResNet, Vision Transformers)—are transforming technology. Under the hood, over 95% of all computation in an AI model consists of Matrix Multiplications (GEMM):

\[Y = W \cdot X + B\]

Where \(W\) is the matrix of learned weights and \(X\) is the input data.

docs.title: 🧠 Why Neural Networks Are Naturally Error-Resilient
docs.text:
Unlike bank databases, neural networks are inherently statistical and probabilistic: 1. Redundancy: Deep networks have millions or billions of parameters. If one weight multiplication is \(1\%\) off, dozens of neighboring neurons compensate naturally. 2. Non-Linear Activations (ReLU & GELU): Functions like \(\text{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z)\) prune away negative noise automatically. 3. Quantization Tolerance: Modern AI models already run on 8-bit integers (INT8) or 4-bit floats (FP4) with zero loss of classification accuracy!

graph LR
    Input["Input Image (Golden Retriever)"] --> Layer1["Conv2D Layer 1<br/>(Inexact Multipliers)"]
    Layer1 --> Layer2["Hidden Layers<br/>(99% Accuracy Arithmetic)"]
    Layer2 --> Output["Output: 'Golden Retriever (99.7% confidence)'"]

docs.title: ⚡ The Massive Energy Savings for AI Chips
docs.text:
When an edge AI chip (in your phone, drone, or smart camera) switches from exact multipliers to Approximate Multipliers (such as DRUM or AC-4:2 Compressors):

AI Network Task Exact Top-1 Accuracy Inexact Top-1 Accuracy Multiplier Energy Saved ResNet-50 Image Classification (ImageNet) \(76.1\%\) \(75.8\%\) \(58\%\) Energy Saved MobileNetV2 Mobile Object Recognition \(71.8\%\) \(71.4\%\) \(62\%\) Energy Saved YOLOv8 Real-time Drone Obstacle Detection \(89.4\%\text{ mAP}\) \(89.1\%\text{ mAP}\) \(54\%\) Energy Saved

A drop of just \(0.3\%\) in accuracy allows the drone to fly twice as long on a single battery charge!

docs.title: Why Human Eyes and Ears Forgive Inexact Math
docs.text:
Have you ever wondered why JPEG pictures take up only \(1/10\)th of the file size of raw uncompressed photos, yet they look virtually identical?

The secret lies in human biology and perceptual noise masking.

docs.title: 👁️ Biology 101: The Human Visual System
docs.text:
Human eyes are not perfect digital video cameras. Our retina and visual cortex have built-in limitations: 1. Luminance vs. Chrominance: We are very sensitive to brightness differences, but much less sensitive to slight color shifts in high-frequency patterns. 2. Spatial Contrast Sensitivity: Our eyes cannot resolve micro-pixel variations when adjacent pixels change rapidly. 3. Temporal Integration: At 60 frames per second, tiny 1-frame pixel errors blur smoothly into motion.

graph TD
    Raw["Raw 4K Video (Exact Math)<br/>Gigabytes of Data, Hot Phone"] --> Filter["Approximate Image Filter<br/>Lower bits truncated"]
    Filter --> Display["Screen Output (0.4% Numerical Error)"]
    Display --> Eye["Human Retina / Visual Cortex"]
    Eye --> Brain["Perceived Image: 100% Crisp & Beautiful!"]

docs.title: 🖼️ The 2D Convolution Mystery
docs.text:
When your phone applies a blur filter, an edge detector, or a portrait mode effect, it performs a mathematical operation called 2D Convolution:

\[\text{Pixel}_{\text{new}}(x, y) = \sum_{i=-1}^{1} \sum_{j=-1}^{1} \text{Image}(x+i, y+j) \times \text{Kernel}(i, j)\]

For a 12-Megapixel photo, this means doing over 100 million multiplications and additions!

  • In an Exact Processor: Every one of those 100 million multiplications calculates the carry propagation down to bit zero.
  • In an Inexact Processor (e.g. TOSAM or DRUM): Lower bits are truncated, using \(60\%\) less energy. The resulting image has a \(\text{PSNR} > 38\text{ dB}\), meaning the differences are completely invisible to the human eye!

docs.title: 🎧 The Same Thing Happens in Audio
docs.text:
When you listen to Spotify or Apple Music, the audio stream has already discarded high-frequency sound waves that human ears cannot hear (the psychoacoustic model).

Using approximate adders and multipliers in audio filters (such as equalizer bass/treble DSPs) saves battery without degrading acoustic fidelity.

docs.title: Approximation Paradigms Across the Stack
docs.text:
Approximate computing techniques span from the circuit level up to the system architecture.

graph TD
    L1[System / Algorithmic Level] --> L2[Microarchitecture Level]
    L2 --> L3[Logic & Gate Level]
    L3 --> L4[Physical & Voltage Level]

    L1 -.->|Task skipping / Early stop| App[Image/DNN QoS]
    L2 -.->|LOD windowing / Speculation| Arch[DRUM / RoBA / CORDIC]
    L3 -.->|Inexact compressors / LPC| Gate[4:2 Compressors / Truncation]
    L4 -.->|Voltage Over-scaling| Phys[VOS / Near-Threshold]

docs.title: A. Static & Dynamic Truncation
docs.text:
• Static Truncation (Fixed-width): Omission of \(k\) lower-order partial product columns.
  • Dynamic Truncation (DRUM / Segmented): Dynamically detecting the most-significant active window of bits using Leading-One Detectors (LOD).

docs.title: B. Inexact Logic & Compressor Simplification
docs.text: • Replacing full adders and 4:2 / 5:2 compressors with truth-table modifications that eliminate complex XOR trees and reduce critical path delay.

docs.title: C. Speculative Arithmetic & Carry Truncation
docs.text: • Breaking long carry-propagation paths by calculating sums based on a short look-ahead window, accepting occasional carry mispredictions.

docs.title: D. Logarithmic & Power-of-Two Approximations
docs.text: • Converting linear multiplication into additions in the logarithm domain (e.g. Mitchell's algorithm, RoBA), replacing multiplier arrays with shifters and simple adders.

docs.title: 2. Dynamic Voltage & Quality Adaptation
docs.text:
• Voltage Over-Scaling (VOS): Operating circuits below nominal supply voltage to save quadratic power (\(P \propto V^2\)), where timing violations are confined to lower-significance logic paths.
  • Runtime QoS Adaptation: Dynamically scaling arithmetic truncation levels based on battery state, frame rate targets, or temperature envelopes.

docs.title: How Do We Grade Mistakes? (Error Metrics Made Easy)
docs.text:
When a regular calculator gives the wrong answer, it gets an F. In approximate computing, we design circuits that make deliberate small mistakes. But how do we know if a mistake is "good and safe" or "catastrophic"?

We use statistical error metrics! Let's explain them using simple, everyday analogies.

docs.title: 🍕 1. Mean Error Distance (MED) — "The Pizza Slice Test"
docs.text:
Imagine you order a pizza with 100 slices. - If the restaurant gives you 99 slices on Monday (1 slice error) - And 101 slices on Tuesday (1 slice error) - And 100 slices on Wednesday (0 slice error)

Your average absolute mistake is: $\(\text{Average Error} = \frac{1 + 1 + 0}{3} = 0.67\text{ slices}\)$

In circuits, Mean Error Distance (MED) is the average difference between what the approximate chip calculated and what an exact computer would have produced:

\[\text{MED} = \frac{1}{N} \sum |Y_{\text{approx}} - Y_{\text{exact}}|\]

Rule of Thumb: A smaller MED means the circuit stays very close to the true answer on average.

docs.title: 📊 2. Mean Relative Error Distance (MRED) — "The Dollar Test"
docs.text:
Think about these two mistakes: 1. Being off by \(10** when buying a **\)20,000 car (a tiny \(0.05\%\) mistake — nobody cares!). 2. Being off by \(10** when buying a **\)1 candy bar (a \(1000\%\) mistake — huge disaster!).

Because numbers have different scales, we calculate the relative percentage error:

\[\text{Relative Error} = \frac{|\text{Mistake}|}{\text{True Value}}\]

Taking the average over all calculations gives us Mean Relative Error Distance (MRED):

\[\text{MRED} = \frac{1}{N} \sum \frac{|Y_{\text{approx}} - Y_{\text{exact}}|}{|Y_{\text{exact}}|}\]

High-School Physics Tip: In image processing and audio, keeping \(\text{MRED} < 2\%\) makes the noise completely invisible to humans!

docs.title: 💥 3. Worst-Case Error (WCE) — "The Ceiling"
docs.text:
What is the biggest possible blunder this circuit can ever make in the worst possible scenario?

\[\text{WCE} = \max |Y_{\text{approx}} - Y_{\text{exact}}|\]

If a 16-bit multiplier has \(\text{WCE} = 64\), you are guaranteed that no matter what crazy numbers you multiply, the answer will never be off by more than 64 (out of \(4,294,967,295\)!).

docs.title: 📸 4. PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio) — "Image Crispness Score"
docs.text:
When you filter or compress a photo, engineers use PSNR (measured in decibels, dB) to measure picture quality:

PSNR > 40 dB  :  Flawless crystal clear (Identical to original)
PSNR 30–40 dB :  Excellent quality (Instagram / YouTube HD standard)
PSNR 20–30 dB :  Noticeable grain or compression blur
PSNR < 20 dB  :  Pixelated mess

Approximate multipliers routinely achieve \(\text{PSNR} > 36\text{ dB}\) while saving \(60\%\) chip energy!

docs.title: ⚖️ Summary Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Metric What It Asks Best Analogy MED On average, how far off is the answer? Average distance from target MRED What is the average percentage mistake? Percent error on a lab report WCE What is the worst mistake that can ever happen? The safety limit / ceiling ER (Error Rate) What percentage of answers have any error at all? How often the coin lands on heads PSNR How beautiful does the filtered picture look? High-definition display rating

docs.title: Error Metrics and Mathematical Bounds
docs.text: In exact digital design, functional correctness is binary. In approximate computing, arithmetic error is treated as a continuous design budget traded against circuit power, delay, and area (PPA).

docs.title: 1. Primary Numerical Error Metrics
docs.text: For an approximate arithmetic block computing \(Y_{approx}(A, B)\) versus the ground-truth exact function \(Y_{exact}(A, B)\) over an input distribution \(S\):

docs.title: Error Distance (\(ED\))
docs.text: \[ED(A, B) = |Y_{approx}(A, B) - Y_{exact}(A, B)|\]

docs.title: Mean Error Distance (\(MED\))
docs.text: \[MED = \frac{1}{|S|} \sum_{(A,B) \in S} |Y_{approx}(A, B) - Y_{exact}(A, B)|\]

docs.title: Mean Relative Error Distance (\(MRED\))
docs.text: $\(MRED = \frac{1}{|S^*|} \sum_{(A,B) \in S^*} \frac{|Y_{approx}(A, B) - Y_{exact}(A, B)|}{|Y_{exact}(A, B)|}\)$ (where \(S^* = \{(A,B) \in S : Y_{exact}(A, B) \neq 0\}\))

docs.title: Normalized Mean Error Distance (\(NMED\))
docs.text: $\(NMED = \frac{MED}{D_{max}}\)$ (where \(D_{max}\) is the maximum possible output magnitude, e.g. \((2^N-1)^2\) for an \(N \times N\) unsigned multiplier).

docs.title: Worst-Case Error (\(WCE\)) / Maximum Error Distance (\(MaxED\))
docs.text: \[WCE = \max_{(A,B) \in S} |Y_{approx}(A, B) - Y_{exact}(A, B)|\]

docs.title: Error Rate (\(ER\))
docs.text: \[ER = \frac{1}{|S|} \sum_{(A,B) \in S} \mathbb{I}(Y_{approx}(A, B) \neq Y_{exact}(A, B))\]

docs.title: Mean Error (\(ME\)) / Bias
docs.text:
\[ME = \frac{1}{|S|} \sum_{(A,B) \in S} (Y_{approx}(A, B) - Y_{exact}(A, B))\]

Design Insight: In iterative accumulation (such as matrix multiplication or FIR convolution), an approximate unit with \(ME \approx 0\) (unbiased) prevents error accumulation drift even when \(ER\) is high.

docs.title: 2. Downstream Application Metrics
docs.text: Domain Key Metric Target Threshold Image Processing Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (\(PSNR\)) \(> 30\text{ dB}\) (Imperceptible degradation) Image Quality Structural Similarity Index (\(SSIM\)) \(> 0.92\) Deep Learning Top-1 Classification Accuracy Drop (\(\Delta Top1\)) \(\le 1.0\%\) Speech / Audio Signal-to-Quantization-Noise Ratio (\(SQNR\)) \(> 25\text{ dB}\)

docs.title: Why Inexact Computing? (The 1% Rule & Battery Life)
docs.text:
Imagine you are watching a 4K movie on your phone. Every second, your phone calculates millions of math operations to color every single pixel on your screen.

Now ask yourself: If one tiny pixel in the corner of the background has a color code of 214 instead of 215, would your eye ever notice?

The answer is never. Human eyes, ears, and brain networks simply cannot detect tiny fractions of a percent difference in sensory data.

graph LR
    ExactMath["Exact Math: 100% Accuracy<br/>100% Battery Drain 🔋🔋🔋"] --> Bad["Every carry bit propagated.<br/>Full power spent on invisible bits."]
    ApproxMath["Inexact Math: 99.2% Accuracy<br/>35% Battery Drain 🔋"] --> Good["Lower bits simplified.<br/>Human eye sees identical picture!"]

docs.title: 🛑 The "Exactness Tax" of Modern Computers
docs.text:
For the last 60 years, computer chips were designed with a strict rule: Zero Error Allowed. Every single addition, subtraction, and multiplication had to produce the 100% mathematically exact result down to the very last binary bit.

While this makes sense for bank account balances or rocket trajectories, it turns out to be tremendously wasteful for: - 🎮 Video games & 3D graphics (Lighting, shadows, physics simulations) - 📸 Phone cameras & image filters (Instagram filters, portrait mode, JPEG compression) - 🤖 Artificial Intelligence & ChatGPT (Neural network matrix multiplications) - 🎧 Music & Voice recognition (Siri, noise cancellation, MP3 audio)

In these fields, computing exact numbers costs up to \(3\times\) more energy and heat, while delivering an output that is completely indistinguishable to human perception!

docs.title: ⚡ How Approximate Computing Fixes This
docs.text:
Approximate computing (also called Inexact Computing) treats mathematical accuracy as a flexible budget rather than a fixed rule:

\[\text{Trade } 1\% \text{ Accuracy} \implies \text{Gain } 50\%–70\% \text{ Energy & Speed Savings}\] 
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|               TRADITIONAL EXACT MULTIPLIER                  |
|  [ 16-bit Multiply ] ---> 256 partial products + Full tree  |
|  Power: 100% | Delay: 1.0 ns | Error: 0.00%                 |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
                              VS
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|               INEXACT / APPROXIMATE MULTIPLIER              |
|  [ 16-bit Multiply ] ---> Lower 6 bits truncated/hacked     |
|  Power: 38%  | Delay: 0.6 ns | Error: 0.8% (Invisible!)     |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: 🎯 Three Places Inexact Computing is Changing the World
1. Smart Wearables & Medical Sensors
docs.text: A smartwatch measuring your heartbeat or an EEG brain patch monitoring for epileptic seizures cannot afford a bulky battery. By using approximate arithmetic, the chip can run continuously for weeks instead of hours without losing diagnostic accuracy.

docs.title: 2. Edge AI & Self-Driving Cars
docs.text: Autonomous drones and cars process dozens of camera frames every second. Inexact neural network accelerators let drones recognize pedestrians and obstacles at 200 frames per second with ultra-low heat.

docs.title: 3. Green Computing & Data Centers
docs.text: Training large AI models burns megawatts of electrical power. Using inexact multipliers in tensor cores slashes electricity bills and global carbon emissions.

docs.title: Adder Carry Propagation Race Lab
docs.text: Explore the fundamental bottleneck of computer arithmetic: the Carry-Propagation Chain.

docs.title: 1. The Ripple-Carry Delay (\(16\times\) Gate Delay)
docs.text: • In a Ripple Carry Adder (RCA), bit 15 cannot compute its final sum until the carry signal ripples across all 15 lower bits.

docs.title: 2. Speculative Carry Prediction (ACA)
docs.text: • Approximate Almost-Correct Adders (ACA) divide the adder into short 4-bit windows. The carry path is cut, reducing the critical delay from \(16\) to only \(4\) gate delays with \(<0.5\%\) error probability!

docs.title: 4:2 Approximate Compressor Playground
docs.text: In high-speed multiplier trees (Wallace and Dadda trees), 4:2 Compressors reduce 4 rows of partial products down to 2 rows.

docs.title: 🔬 Key Insights
docs.text:
1. Gate Count Optimization: Exact 4:2 compressors require 26 standard CMOS transistors. Approximate AC-4:2 compressors eliminate complex internal XOR gates, using only 14 transistors (\(46\%\) area reduction).
  2. Truth Table Accuracy: Across all 32 input state combinations, the approximate compressor matches the exact mathematical result in 28 out of 32 states (\(87.5\%\) exact accuracy), with any rare deviation strictly bounded to \(\pm 1\).

docs.title: CORDIC Rotation Visualizer Lab
docs.text: The CORDIC algorithm computes trigonometric functions and coordinate vector rotations without any multiplier hardware, using only bit-shifts and additions.

docs.title: 🔬 What to Observe
docs.text:
1. Micro-Rotation Convergence: CORDIC rotates the vector using predefined angle steps (\(\theta_i = \arctan(2^{-i}) \in \{45^\circ, 26.56^\circ, 14.04^\circ, 7.12^\circ, \dots\}\)).
  2. Early Termination (Adaptive Pruning): Late iterations contribute tiny fractions of a degree. Stopping early saves clock cycles and dynamic power with \(<0.3^\circ\) phase error.

docs.title: Image Filter & Noise Sandbox Lab
docs.text: In this interactive lab, you can test how inexact multipliers affect real 2D image processing filters in real time.

docs.title: 1. Perceptual Noise Masking
docs.text:
• Try switching between Exact Multiplier and Truncated LSB-4.
  • Notice that even though millions of individual math operations produce slight deviations, the human eye perceives a virtually identical crisp image with \(\text{PSNR} > 38\text{ dB}\).

docs.title: 2. Gaussian Smoothing vs Edge Detection
docs.text:
• Gaussian Blur naturally averages neighbor pixels, making arithmetic errors self-canceling.
  • Sobel Edge Detection computes sharp gradient differences, where error bounds must remain tightly controlled.

docs.title: Approximate Adders Taxonomy
docs.text: Adders form the foundational atomic unit of all arithmetic pipelines. Approximate adders eliminate carry-chain propagation delay or reduce gate count.

docs.title: 1. Classification Taxonomy
docs.text:
graph TD
    A[Approximate Adders] --> S1[1. Speculative / Carry-Lookahead]
    A --> S2[2. Segmented / Lower-Part Approximation]
    A --> S3[3. Inexact Full Adder Cells]
    A --> S4[4. Error-Correctable / Reconfigurable]

    S1 --> D1[ACA / ACA-CSU / ETA]
    S2 --> D2[LOA / LPCA / HEAA]

docs.title: Approximate CORDIC Architectures
docs.text: The Coordinate Rotation Digital Computer (CORDIC) algorithm is widely used to compute trigonometric functions, coordinate rotations, vector magnitudes, and hyperbolic mappings without dedicated multipliers.

docs.title: 1. Approximation Levers in CORDIC
docs.text:
graph TD
    C[Approximate CORDIC] --> M1[1. Angle Iteration Pruning]
    C --> M2[2. Approximate Internal Adders]
    C --> M3[3. Scale-Factor (K) Simplification]
    C --> M4[4. Fully Parallel Unrolled Architectures]

    M1 --> O1[Early termination / Adaptive iterations]
    M2 --> O2[Speculative adders in X/Y/Z datapath]
    M3 --> O3[Shift-and-add scale constant approximation]
    M4 --> O4[Pipelined constant rotation schedule]

docs.title: 2. Key Techniques & Design Rules
docs.text:
1. Iteration Elimination: High-order iterations (\(i > N/2\)) contribute micro-rotations. Pruning them reduces latency linearly with bounded phase error.
  2. Datapath Truncation: Lower bits in intermediate \(X_i, Y_i\) registers experience diminishing significance, enabling lower-part truncation adders.
  3. Scale Factor (\(K\)) Folding: Conventional CORDIC requires multiplying by \(K = \prod \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2^{-2i}}} \approx 0.60725\). Approximate CORDIC merges scaling directly into the terminal shift stages.

docs.title: Approximate Multipliers Taxonomy
docs.text: Multipliers dominate the energy and silicon area budgets in digital signal processing (DSP) and neural network accelerators.

docs.title: Track 2: AI & Edge Hardware Accelerator
docs.text:
This roadmap guides you through building ultra-efficient AI accelerators using approximate multipliers for neural networks like ResNet, YOLO, and Vision Transformers.

graph LR

docs.title: Milestone 1: Quantization & Error Sensitivity
docs.text:
• Understand how floating-point weights (FP32) are converted to 8-bit integers (INT8).
  • Identify which neural network layers (e.g. early convolutional layers vs final classifier) are most sensitive to approximation.

docs.title: Milestone 2: Emulating Inexact Multiplications in Python
docs.text: • Implement custom PyTorch torch.autograd.Function operators that plug in DRUM or RoBA multiplier models during inference.

docs.title: Milestone 3: Benchmark Accuracy on ImageNet / CIFAR-10
docs.text:
• Run full inference passes on standard image datasets.
  • Measure Top-1 classification accuracy drop and ensure \(\Delta \text{Acc} \le 0.5\%\).

docs.title: Track 1: The Circuit Hacker (Verilog & Hardware)
docs.text:
Welcome to the Circuit Hacker Track! This roadmap is designed for students and aspiring silicon engineers who want to design synthesizable digital circuits in Verilog.

graph TD
    Step1["1. Binary Logic & Full Adders"] --> Step2["2. Build an Inexact 4:2 Compressor"]
    Step2 --> Step3["3. Assemble an 8x8 Approximate Multiplier"]
    Step3 --> Step4["4. Simulate with Icarus Verilog"]
    Step4 --> Step5["5. Synthesize into 45nm Silicon Gates"]

docs.title: Stage 1: The Basic Gates & Truth Tables
docs.text:
• Understand AND, OR, XOR logic gates.
  • Build an exact Full Adder: $\(\text{Sum} = A \oplus B \oplus C_{in}, \quad C_{out} = (A \cdot B) + (C_{in} \cdot (A \oplus B))\)$

docs.title: Stage 2: The Inexact Hack
docs.text:
• Look at the 4:2 compressor truth table.
  • Identify output combinations that cost 5 extra transistors.
  • Modify the Boolean equation to simplify the gate count while keeping error rate under \(5\%\).

docs.title: Stage 3: Verilog RTL Implementation
docs.text:
• Write clean, synthesizable Verilog for your approximate multiplier.
  • Write a self-checking testbench (tb_top.v) that tests all 65,536 input combinations and calculates total error distance.

docs.title: Stage 4: Synthesis & ASIC Area
docs.text:
• Synthesize your Verilog code using open PDKs (FreePDK45 / ASAP7).
  • Compare your silicon area and power consumption against the exact multiplier!
